title: May I be a medicine
hookLine: honey on a spoon, ginger in a mug; Shantideva wishes to be the medicine itself
tomorrow: medicine was one. what else does he wish to be?

lines: HE WISHES TO BE THE MEDICINE.
cards: A spoonful of honey for a sore throat. A mug of ginger tea, too hot to drink, with steam that clears your nose before the first sip. The bitter little pill somebody cut in half for you when you were small.

Medicine has a taste, and it usually comes with a person: whoever stood at the stove, or held out the spoon. So, yesterday's riddle: what does Shantideva wish he were, that you'd swallow? He wishes to be the medicine.

teach.b: Chapter three, right after rejoicing. Shantideva makes a run of wishes, and here is one of them. For everyone in the world who is sick, may I be the medicine, the doctor and the nurse, until the sickness never comes back.
Notice there are three roles, and he wants all of them. The doctor knows what's wrong. The nurse stays through the night.
And the medicine is the strangest wish of all.
It gets used up. It disappears into the person who needs it, and nobody thanks the pill.

teach.h: RAIN AS FOOD IN A FAMINE.
teach.b: The very next verse pushes further: in a famine, may I fall like rain as food and drink. This is an aspiration, a wish said with the whole heart, the kind the awakening mind runs on.
It doesn't claim he can cure anyone yet.

teach.h: A WISH THAT POINTS A LIFE.
teach.b: It points his whole life toward being of use. And it reaches the ordinary scale, too.
Nobody has to be a doctor to be someone's medicine: the cup of tea, the honey on the spoon, the person who sits with you while the pill works. May I be the medicine.

how: Mahayana Buddhists recite verses from this part of chapter three as aspirations, and the Medicine Buddha, Bhaisajyaguru, is honored in East Asian and Tibetan Buddhism as a Buddha of healing.

games.q: what does “may i be a medicine” mean?
o: a vow to study medicine and become a doctor
wishing to heal and care for anyone who suffers
asking the Buddha for a cure for your own illness

games.q: the medicine verse — tap the pairs.
p: gets used up for someone else

s: Shantideva claims he can already cure every illness
it's an aspiration: a wish that points his life toward being of use, not a claim of power.
he wishes to be the medicine, the doctor and the nurse
all three roles, until the sickness never comes back.
being someone's medicine requires medical training
the wish reaches ordinary life: a cup of tea, a spoon of honey, someone who stays.

games.q: your roommate has the flu and you have a big deadline. what fits Shantideva's wish?
o: stay away completely; you can't be useful if you get sick too.
drop the deadline and stay by her bed all day.
leave tea and soup at her door, check in by text, and keep working.
games.why: the wish is to be medicine where you are. a cup by the door and a message are small, real ways of being someone's medicine.

practice: If you have a warm drink or even a glass of water, hold it in both hands and take one slow sip, noticing the warmth or the cool on your tongue. Then bring one person to mind who isn't feeling well, in body or in heart.
Let the next sips be for them, and see one small way you could help them feel better.

wordCard.voice: May I be a medicine: Shantideva's wish to be medicine, doctor and nurse for all who are sick, until no one is.

orig.note: Sanskrit: medicine, remedy. The same word is in the name of the Medicine Buddha, Bhaisajyaguru.

carryVoice: Your line: may I be the medicine. Most medicine comes in a cup and a kind hand. Twelve days into the poem.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 3.7-3.8 (may I be the medicine, the doctor and the nurse; in famine, may I become food and drink)
